column2: Question (plain words)
column3: The one fact to say first
column6: If unsure ask
column7: What it adds to the framework

column2: What is it, who uses it, and where?
column7: Feeds every line below. Answer as many of 2-21 as you can from this before asking any.

column2: Does it diagnose, treat, prevent or monitor a health problem, or go inside the body?
column3: Health products have their own rules, and they decide early how heavy the road is.
column4: iso-13485, fda-human-factors, iec-62366-usability; FDA device classification (not in library yet)
column6: What claim would the box make: wellness, or treating something?
column7: Medical road: FDA class decides the path. Design controls and usability records. Refer to a regulatory professional early.

column2: Does it fly, or go on an aircraft, drone or spacecraft?
column3: Aviation parts follow a stricter quality system and the aviation authority.
column6: Who would install it?
column7: AS9100-style records and traceability.

column2: Is it part of a car, truck or other vehicle, or mounted on one?
column3: Vehicle suppliers usually work to the automotive quality system.
column6: Is it sold to the car maker, or as an add-on to drivers?
column7: AIAG core tools: PPAP-style records, process FMEA, control plan. Add-ons to drivers stay lighter.

column2: Will the government or the military buy it?
column3: Selling to the government uses a separate registration; ordinary customers do not need it.
column6: Has a government buyer asked about it?
column7: Registration road. Military specs only from question 6.

column2: (Military only) Will it see rough handling, weather or vibration, sit near radios, or ship in military packaging?
column3: Military buyers name test standards in the contract.
column6: Does the contract name any standard?
column7: Only the standards the contract names. Test plan per standard.

column2: Does it plug into the wall?
column3: Mains power usually means testing by a recognized lab before stores will take it.
column6: Will it have a cord or a charger?
column7: Listing by a recognized lab (UL or similar). Safety test plan. Engineer for the power design.

column2: Does it have a battery, a circuit board or software?
column3: Electronics bring their own risks: heat, battery safety, static.
column4: ul-standards, iec-esd, tek-precompliance, digikey, jlcpcb, macrofab
column6: What makes it work?
column7: Electronics road (sop-gateways POWER). Battery and static checks.

column2: Does it send or receive anything wirelessly (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, radio), or have fast digital electronics?
column3: Anything that radiates needs FCC authorization to be sold in the U.S.
column6: Will it connect to a phone?
column7: FCC path. A pre-certified radio module saves cost. Pre-compliance test early.

column2: Is it a machine, or part of one, used in a shop or factory?
column3: Industrial machines have their own electrical standard and guarding.
column6: Who runs it: a worker on a line, or someone at home?
column7: Machine safety and guarding. Industrial enclosures.

column2: Is it used outdoors, washed, rained on or submerged?
column3: If it has to survive water, the case and switches must be sealed.
column6: Where will it live?
column7: An IP or NEMA rating as a requirement. Seal test in the test plan.

column2: Is it made for, or likely to be used by, children under 12?
column3: Children's products need third-party testing and a certificate.
column4: cpsc-small-business, cpsc-regulatory-robot; CPSIA children's products (not in library yet)
column6: Would a parent buy it for a child?
column7: Third-party lab testing and a children's product certificate. Small-parts and lead checks.

column2: Does it touch food, drink, the mouth, or skin for long periods, or is it worn?
column3: Materials that touch food or skin have rules about what they can be made of.
column4: cpsc-regulatory-robot, ansur2-design-data, niosh-ergonomics-overview; FDA food-contact (not in library yet)
column6: What is it made of where it touches?
column7: Material choice becomes a requirement. Supplier material certificates.

column2: Is it held, gripped, lifted or used over and over by hand?
column3: Grip, weight and repeat use decide whether people keep using it.
column6: How long does someone use it at a time?
column7: Ergonomics check sheet. User trial in the test plan.

column2: Could it hurt someone: moving parts, blades, heat, pressure, stored energy?
column3: Products that can injure need a deeper failure look, and an engineer on that part.
column6: What is the worst thing that could happen with it?
column7: Quality depth for the product overall: light (about 5 items), ordinary (20-30) or deep. Separately, any area where a hidden defect could injure someone or start a fire gets a deep failure look for that area (failure, cause, effect, how it's caught, how it's prevented, engineer review), even when the rest is ordinary. Propose it; they confirm. Engineer referral for the hazard. A real injury hazard also brings the company-liability question forward.

column2: Will it be shipped by a carrier, or dropped in normal use?
column3: Shipping is a test of its own; boxes get dropped.
column6: Will you mail it to customers?
column7: Drop and package test in the test plan.

column2: Where will it be sold: friends, your own website, Amazon, Walmart or Lowe's, or outside the U.S.?
column3: Big stores and marketplaces have supplier rules; other countries have their own marks.
column4: Stores: retail group, gs1-barcodes, sheet-retail. Outside U.S.: cenelec, iec-electrical; EU CE marking (not in library yet)
column6: Where would you like to see it first?
column7: Retail road: barcodes, supplier requirements, insurance often required by the store. Export marks.

column2: Has a customer, contract or buyer named a standard or certification?
column3: We keep our own quality list either way; a named standard is added only when someone requires it.
column4: Only the named standard (look it up; assist or the standards body)
column5: The standards shelf (our own sheets still apply)
column7: That standard's records and tests, nothing more.

column2: Do you want a company so the product's liability sits on it instead of on you?
column3: A business entity, set up properly, can put the liability for the product on the business. It is not automatic.
column6: (sop-gateways BUSINESS ENTITY)
column7: Formation tasks. If no: one-line checks later, e.g. product liability insurance instead.

column2: What are your thoughts on a patent?
column3: Showing or selling it can make some protection harder to get later. You can still choose not to file.
column4: inventor and legal groups: uspto-inventor-hub, uspto-iac, patent-pro-bono, patent-law-school-clinics, uspto-provisional, google-patents
column6: (sop-gateways PATENT)
column7: Patent options ladder: package for an attorney, free help, file it yourself, don't file.

column2: Will the next step need someone else's money?
column3: Someone else's money comes with that person's rules.
column4: funding group for the kind named (sbir, sba-lender, angel-groups, kickstarter-handbook)
column6: (sop-gateways OUTSIDE MONEY)
column7: Funding road for that kind of money only.

column2: Does it attach to, fit, or depend on another company's product or brand (a robot, a phone, a car model, a tool system)?
column3: Selling something made for another company's product raises their name, their specs and their warranty. Using their name to say what it fits is often allowed; using it as your brand is not.
column4: trademark-basics; uspto-patent-overview (their patents on the product it fits); the maker's published accessory or developer program, if any (search their official site)
column6: Do they publish its sizes, weights and attachment points, or are you guessing from videos?
column7: Brand line: how the product is named ('fits X' vs a name using X), checked against trademark-basics. Compatibility: which specs are official vs guessed (guesses stay open, never used as limits). Warranty: could using it void the host product's warranty. Route: the maker's accessory or partner program, if one exists. Their patents: a quick look before showing it. Lawyer if their name goes on the box.

column2: Is it sold into a particular industry, or used somewhere unusual: railroad, mining, marine, oil and gas, a food plant, a hospital, washdown, a hazardous area?
column3: Many industries have their own rules for equipment that the common standards miss. Railroad is one: rail buyers have their own specs for electronics, remote controls, enclosures and washdown.
column4: Industry search (sop-resource-map step 4): search that industry's own specs for this kind of product, then add what turns up as found, not yet checked
column5: Nothing extra; the common groups cover it
column6: Who buys it, and where exactly does it get used?
column7: That industry's spec as a requirement, with its source. Record the search and date even when nothing turns up.

column2: Does it have electronics, or will it be sold in Europe or California?
column3: Electronics and some materials have rules on lead and other restricted substances. Suppliers usually supply the paperwork.
column6: What is it made of, and where would it be sold first?
column7: Supplier material declarations on the BOM. Prop 65 warning check if sold in California.

column2: Does it have a lithium battery, or will it ship by air?
column3: Lithium batteries have their own shipping tests and carrier rules before anything goes in a box.
column4: un-38-3-battery-shipping (not in library yet); carrier rules
column6: What kind of battery, and is it built in?
column7: Battery shipping test and labels before the first shipment. Pairs with row 16.
